title: Jotai v2.20: Rework Store Building Blocks for High-Throughput Performance and Sets the Stage for v3
gist: Jotai v2.20.0 reverses a performance regression caused by the WeakMap that had been introduced to make its store building blocks extensible, swapping it for parameter passing. Creator Daishi Kato frames the release as the last step before Jotai v3, whose stated plan is to redesign the building blocks array, drop CommonJS builds, drop React below 18 and remove setSelf — with atomFamily already deprecated in favour of the separate jotai-family package.

themes.theme: The WeakMap regression and its reversal

insights.claim: Jotai's store building blocks caused a reported performance regression whose major cause was the WeakMap introduced to make those building blocks more flexible, and v2.20.0 fixes it by swapping WeakMap for passing everything as parameters instead.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Extensibility mechanisms carry measurable runtime cost in hot paths — a concrete case where an abstraction had to be unwound to recover throughput.
insights.quote: Someone reported a performance regression, and the major reason was the use of WeakMap, which had been introduced to make the building blocks more flexible (#3280). The fix swaps the WeakMap approach for passing everything as parameters instead.

insights.claim: Jotai v2.20.0 is framed around a single theme — improving performance in high-throughput scenarios — and lands a small set of internal changes including avoiding getInternalBuildingBlock, Rev3 type narrowing for onMount hooks, and lazy hooks in ensureAtomState for new atom state.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: The release is narrow and internal — application teams gain throughput without migration work, which is why adoption should be near-frictionless.
insights.quote: Jotai v2.20.0 centres on a single theme: improving performance in high-throughput scenarios.

insights.claim: Kato characterises the parameter-passing fix as 'not super clean, but fits with my mental model', explicitly trading architectural elegance for maintainer comprehensibility in a library he must keep evolving.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Single-maintainer libraries optimise for the maintainer's mental model, which is a real constraint on how fast such projects can absorb complexity — a bus-factor consideration for anyone depending on them.
insights.quote: Kato described the solution as "not super clean, but fits with my mental model,"

insights.claim: Two follow-up patch releases, v2.20.1 and v2.20.2, shipped already to address further edge cases, indicating the building-blocks rework surfaced more than the single regression it targeted.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Rapid patch cadence after an internals rework is the standard signal to wait a release cycle before upgrading a production dependency.

themes.theme: Building blocks: an API design bet from v2.12 to v2.15

insights.claim: The building blocks idea first arrived in Jotai v2.12.0 more than a year earlier, exposing internals specifically so ecosystem libraries such as jotai-effect and jotai-scope could extend the core.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Core libraries exposing internals to support their own plugin ecosystem is the design decision that later constrains their performance — a recurring pattern to watch in dependency selection.
insights.quote: the building blocks idea first arrived in v2.12.0 more than a year ago, exposing some internals so that ecosystem libraries such as jotai-effect and jotai-scope could extend Jotai's core

insights.claim: Kato deliberately rejected letting the store be extended after creation — worrying it could cause mismatched capabilities over time — and instead accepts customisation only at the moment a store is built, an API he judged both flexible and hard to misuse by around v2.15.0.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Build-time customisation over runtime extension is a transferable API design rule for anyone shipping an extensible library: it bounds the capability matrix you must support.
insights.quote: Rather than letting the store be extended after creation, which he worried could cause mismatched capabilities over time, Kato chose to accept customisation at the moment a store is built.

insights.claim: The breaking label on Jotai v2.20 applies only to internal building blocks used by library authors, not to typical application code — creating and using a store looks exactly as it did before.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Breakage is concentrated in the ecosystem tier, so the upgrade risk sits with plugin maintainers rather than product teams — check your jotai-* dependencies, not your app code.
insights.quote: The breaking label applies to the internal building blocks used by library authors, not to typical application code.
insights.locator: 'For most developers the everyday API is untouched'

insights.claim: The downstream impact is visible in jotai-devtools v0.14.0, which added support for INTERNAL_buildStoreRev3 and dropped older versions to stay compatible — a forced version cliff for anyone using the devtools.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Internal-API churn propagates as hard version pins across the plugin ecosystem — the practical cost of depending on libraries that expose internals.

insights.claim: atomFamily is deprecated ahead of Jotai v3 in favour of the separate jotai-family package, and teams still on Jotai v1 are directed to the official v2 migration guide.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Core-to-satellite-package migration is the deprecation path being used here — a migration cost to schedule before v3, not after.
insights.quote: those relying on atomFamily should note it is deprecated ahead of v3 in favour of the jotai-family package
insights.locator: 'Teams still on Jotai v1 should consult'

insights.claim: Kato's outlined Jotai v3 plan explicitly includes redesigning the building blocks array structure — the very internals v2.20 just reworked — alongside dropping CommonJS builds, dropping support for React below 18, and removing the setSelf option.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: The internals being stabilised now are scheduled to change again in v3 — plugin authors should treat v2.20 compatibility work as temporary.
insights.quote: Kato has outlined a v3 plan that explicitly includes a redesign of the building blocks array structure, the very internals this release touches, alongside dropping CommonJS builds, dropping support for React below 18, and removing the setSelf option.
insights.locator: 'Direct community reaction to the point release has been muted'

insights.claim: A contributor argued dropping CommonJS should not even be a question since essentially all Jotai users run a bundler that supports ESM, but Kato's reply pushed back by pointing to server-side rendering users who still need consideration.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: SSR is the reason CJS support persists across the JavaScript ecosystem long after bundler users have moved on — the constraint to check before assuming an ESM-only migration is safe.
insights.quote: Regarding dropping CJS - I don't think this should even be a question. 99,9999% of Jotai users are using some kind of bundler, all of which support ESM just fine.

insights.claim: Suggestions to loosen Jotai's coupling with React and court other frameworks were met with a firmly React-first stance from the maintainer, closing off framework-agnostic expansion as a growth path.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Jotai's addressable market is deliberately capped at React — relevant when comparing it to framework-agnostic state libraries competing for the same mindshare.
insights.quote: Suggestions to loosen Jotai's coupling with React and court other frameworks were met with a firmly React-first stance.
insights.locator: 'Kato's reply highlights that server-side rendering users'

themes.theme: Positioning in the React state-management field

insights.claim: Jotai remains the leading atomic state option for React while sitting behind Zustand — also created by Daishi Kato — in raw downloads, meaning the same maintainer owns both the leader and the leading challenger in the category.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Concentration of a whole category's leadership under one maintainer is a single-point dependency risk for the React ecosystem worth noting in tech due diligence.
insights.quote: Jotai remains the leading atomic option while sitting behind Kato's own Zustand in raw downloads.

insights.claim: The project frames the mental-model split explicitly: Jotai is bottom-up atoms akin to Recoil, Zustand is a single top-down store closer to Redux, and Kato's proxy-based Valtio targets a third model again.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: A clean three-way taxonomy for evaluating React state libraries — pick by mental model rather than by benchmark, since the same author ships all three.
insights.quote: The project's own comparison frames Jotai as bottom-up atoms akin to Recoil, whereas Zustand offers a single top-down store closer to Redux, and Kato's proxy-based Valtio targets a different mental model again.
